intro: Everyday idioms (moods, relationships, money, surprises, conversation) are everywhere in series, podcasts and conversations between friends. At C1 you need to understand them instantly and use a few of them with no mistakes in form.
objectifs: Understand about forty everyday idioms, organised by theme.
Avoid word-for-word translations of idioms from your own language.
Master their grammar: what can change (tense, possessive), what cannot, and why the passive is almost impossible.
Recognise shortened proverbs (“Speak of the devil…”, “When in Rome…”) and British and American variants.

texte: Many emotion idioms use images of the body or the sky. They are very common in speech and messages; in formal writing, a simple adjective is usually better (delighted, nervous, exhausted).

lignes: be extremely happy, in a dreamy way
be at the end of your tether (BrE) / rope (AmE)
have no patience or energy left
suddenly become too nervous to do something

exemples: She was over the moon when she got the scholarship.
He got cold feet a week before the wedding.
He suddenly became too nervous to go ahead.

texte: These idioms describe how well people get on, their conflicts and their reconciliations. The image can be surprising: “get on like a house on fire” (get on extremely well) has nothing to do with danger.

lignes: get on like a house on fire
My mum and my wife get on like a house on fire.
We don't always see eye to eye on money.
After the argument, she gave me the cold shoulder.
rub sb up the wrong way (BrE) / rub sb the wrong way (AmE)
His tone really rubs me up the wrong way.
talk openly to end a tension
We had a long talk to clear the air.
end a quarrel and become friends again
The two brothers finally buried the hatchet.

exemples: We don't see eye to eye on politics, but we're still close.
“See eye to eye” is mostly used in the negative.

texte: Money idioms are essential for talking about the cost of living; idioms of time and surprise appear in every story.

lignes: cost an arm and a leg
Rent in Vancouver costs an arm and a leg.
have just enough money to live
They work two jobs to make ends meet.
We'll have to tighten our belts this year.
spend a lot on something special
We splashed out on a new sofa.
They travelled around Asia on a shoestring.
He called me out of the blue after ten years.
I only eat meat once in a blue moon.
We got to the station in the nick of time.
something bad that has a good result
Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
the final problem that makes you lose patience
The noise at 3 a.m. was the last straw.

exemples: With two children and one salary, it's hard to make ends meet.
“Make” changes form; the rest is fixed.
Missing the bus turned out to be a blessing in disguise.
The bad event had a good result.

texte: These idioms comment on conversation itself: telling a secret, getting to the point, making a social mistake, guessing right. Note the variants: “beat about the bush” (BrE) / “beat around the bush” (AmE), “put your foot in it” (BrE) / “put your foot in your mouth” (AmE), “take sth with a pinch of salt” (BrE) / “with a grain of salt” (AmE).

lignes: spill the beans / let the cat out of the bag
Who spilled the beans about the party?
Stop beating about the bush and tell me.
Let me cut to the chase: I'm leaving.
hit the nail on the head
You've hit the nail on the head.
I put my foot in it by mentioning his ex.
I wanted to argue, but I bit my tongue.
take sth with a pinch of salt
Take online reviews with a pinch of salt.

exemples: I really put my foot in it when I asked about her job.
The possessive agrees with the subject (my, his, her…).

sections.titre: The grammar of idioms and shortened proverbs
texte: What changes: the tense of the verb (spill / spilled / has spilled the beans) and the possessive, which agrees with the subject (I bit my tongue, she bit her tongue). What does not change: nouns, articles, prepositions and word order. You cannot say “spill the bean” or “a house in fire”.
The passive is almost always impossible: “The beans were spilled by Tom” loses the idiomatic meaning and sounds like a joke. Keep the active voice.

Native speakers often shorten a well-known proverb: “Speak of the devil!”, “When in Rome…” (do as the Romans do), “Too many cooks…” (spoil the broth). Recognising the beginning is enough to understand the reference.
exemples: Speak of the devil! We were just talking about you.
Said when someone arrives just as you mention them (the full proverb ends “and he shall appear”).
I don't usually eat insects, but when in Rome…
A reference to “When in Rome, do as the Romans do”.
sections.note: Past of “spill”: spilled (everywhere) or spilt (mainly British).

formule: Verb in the right tense + fixed chunk (nouns, articles, prepositions unchanged) + matching possessive; active voice; informal or neutral register
prononciation: Stress falls on the words that carry the image: over the MOON, a BLESSing in disGUISE, the last STRAW.
“an arm and a leg” is linked: /ən ˈɑːm ən ə ˈleɡ/, with “and” reduced to /ən/.
In shortened proverbs, the voice stays up (rising or level tone) on the last word: “When in ROME…”
erreurs: It costs the eyes of the head.
It costs an arm and a leg.
A translation from French; in English it is an arm and a leg.
Stop turning around the pot.
Stop beating about / around the bush.
The English idiom is “beat about the bush”.
That was the drop that overflowed the vase.
That was the last straw.
From “the straw that broke the camel's back”.
Talk of the wolf!
Speak / Talk of the devil!
In English it is the devil, not the wolf.
They get on like a house in fire.
They get on like a house on fire.
Fixed preposition: “on fire”.
I have butterflies in the stomach.
I have butterflies in my stomach.
English uses a possessive with parts of the body.
The beans were spilled by my sister.
My sister spilled the beans.
Idioms are very rarely used in the passive.
She's in the seventh sky.
She's on cloud nine. / She's over the moon.
English says “cloud nine”.

dialogue.contexte: Two friends have coffee in Liège; one describes a difficult week.
lignes: Honestly, I'm at the end of my tether. My landlord put the rent up out of the blue.
No patience left; a sudden rise.
Again? Rent here costs an arm and a leg already.
I know. And then my boss gave me the cold shoulder all week. That was the last straw.
He ignored her; the final problem.
Did you talk to him? Sometimes you need to clear the air.
Talk openly to end the tension.
I did. I didn't beat about the bush. And guess what? He offered me a transfer to the Namur office.
So the whole thing was a blessing in disguise!
A bad situation with a good result.
Exactly. Cheaper rent, and a team I get on with like a house on fire. It's a weight off my shoulders.
Great relationships and a great relief.

mots: They were over the moon with the news.
She got cold feet before the interview.
sudden nervousness that stops you acting
We rarely see eye to eye on music.
He gave his neighbour the cold shoulder.
Many students struggle to make ends meet.
have just enough money to live
They started the business on a shoestring.
a very small budget (on a shoestring)
The offer came out of the blue.
The delay was the last straw.
the final problem that makes you lose patience
Don't spill the beans about the surprise.
Take his promises with a pinch of salt.

exercices.consigne: Explain the idiom in plain English.
items: once in a blue moon
very rarely
in the nick of time
just in time
bury the hatchet
end a quarrel and make peace
let off steam
release strong feelings or energy

exercices.consigne: Write the missing word of the idiom.
items: Let me cut to the ___: we can't afford it.
chase
You've hit the nail on the ___.
head
I wanted to answer back, but I bit my ___.
tongue
With prices rising, we all have to tighten our ___.
belts
They get on like a house ___ fire.
on
My brother put his foot ___ it at dinner.
in

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence, replacing the words in brackets with an idiom from the lesson.
items: She was [extremely happy] with her results.
She was over the moon with her results.
He [suddenly decided not to do it] the day before the race.
He got cold feet the day before the race.
Who [revealed the secret]?
Who spilled the beans? / Who let the cat out of the bag?
We [never agree] with our neighbours.
We never see eye to eye with our neighbours.

exercices.consigne: Correct the mistake (often a translated or altered idiom).
items: This phone costs the eyes of the head.
This phone costs an arm and a leg.
Talk of the wolf, here's Sam!
Speak of the devil, here's Sam!
I always have butterflies in the stomach before exams.
I always have butterflies in my stomach before exams.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with an idiom.
items: Stop avoiding the subject and say it.
Stop beating about the bush (AmE: around the bush) and say it.
With one salary, it's hard to have enough money to live.
With one salary, it's hard to make ends meet.

exercices.consigne: In 4–5 sentences, tell the story of something unexpected that happened to you. Use at least three idioms from the lesson.
items: Example answer

Last year, my company closed its Yaoundé office out of the blue, and I was down in the dumps for weeks. Money was tight, so we had to tighten our belts and live on a shoestring. Then a former colleague called me and offered me a job in a start-up. Looking back, losing that job was a blessing in disguise.

a_retenir: Group idioms by theme (emotions, relationships, money, time, conversation) and learn them in full sentences.
Only the tense and the possessive change; nouns, articles and prepositions are fixed; no passive.
Beware of translating: cost an arm and a leg, beat about the bush, the last straw, speak of the devil.
Know the variants: beat about (BrE) / around (AmE) the bush; a pinch (BrE) / a grain (AmE) of salt; the end of your tether (BrE) / rope (AmE).
